title: MB9-06567
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), his wife XXXX XXXX (co-Appellant) and their children, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated March 19, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), his wife XXXX XXXX (co-Appellant) and their children, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated March 19, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

The Appellants fear the family of the Principal Appellant's first wife in Pakistan. The Principal Appellant and his first wife were married in 2006 in an arranged marriage with which both of them disagreed. The Principal Appellant returned to the United Arab Emirates where he lived and worked. His first wife did not accompany him. His first wife gave birth to their daughter in 2007 in Pakistan. The Principal Appellant returned to Pakistan in XXXX 2008 to meet his daughter and repair the marriage. He was refused access to his daughter. The Principal Appellant returned to the UAE and decided to end his first marriage but did not do so formally. The Principal Appellant met his second wife in XXXX 2008 in the UAE and married her in XXXX 2009. The Appellants allege that starting in XXXX 2008, the Principal Appellant's ex-in-laws have been threatening him and also his new family. After losing their jobs in the UAE and fearing a return to Pakistan, the Appellants travelled to Canada and requested asylum.

The RPD found that the Appellants did not establish the credibility of their claims of threats from the in-laws and also noted that they had returned to Pakistan several times despite their alleged fears. It also found that the co-Appellant had not established a risk to her life as a woman in Pakistan and that XXXX XXXX XXXX diagnosis did not provide the panel with grounds to accept him as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its assessment of the credibility of their claims of harm as a result of the Principal Appellant's dispute with his first wife and that it failed to properly assess the co-Appellant's risk of harm as a woman in Pakistan. The Appellants have not challenged the RPD's decision relating to XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The appeal is denied. The determinative issue is the Appellants' credibility. The Appellants have not established on a balance of probabilities that the Principal Appellant's ex-in-laws have threatened his or his new family's lives. The evidence indicates that the Principal Appellant's ex-wife and her family have pursued the Principal Appellant in the Jirga and court systems to resolve any disputes related to their marital separation. The Appellants have returned to Pakistan many times since 2008 and have not provided acceptable credible reasons for their returns in the context of their alleged fears. The RPD correctly determined that XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection for reasons related to his XXXX diagnosis.

The request that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) admit late new evidence pursuant to RAD Rule 29 is denied. The new evidence is a divorce certificate confirming the end of the Principal Appellant's marriage to his first wife. The Appellants claim that this evidence should trigger a new hearing allowing him to explain the harm that he fears as a result of this divorce. The Appellants believe that all of the evidence should be re-evaluated in light of this confirmed divorce. The Principal Appellant's allegations of harm do not hinge upon the confirmation of a divorce with his wife. The alleged harm is related to a breakdown of the first marriage and incidents that occurred in 2008, and also to the Principal Appellant's second marriage in 2009. The Principal Appellant's Basis of Claim form (BOC) attests to the fact that a divorce in family court was imminent. A certificate confirming the divorce, a fact that was already before the RPD, does not bring new relevant evidence before the RAD and does not justify a re-evaluation of the facts at a new hearing. ANALYSIS Nexus to Convention

The RPD correctly determined that there is no nexus to the Convention. The Appellants allege that the RPD erred by finding that there was no nexus to the convention. They allege that they are part of a particular social group - family members who are at risk of honour crimes. They explain that while the Principal Appellant does not fear gender-based violence, they do fear the consequences of an honour crime, particularly within the context of his Pashtun culture. Being a family at risk of an honour crime is not, in my view, an element that defines membership in a particular social group. In this case, it is an allegation that the Appellants must defend and not any characteristic that ties them to a particular group, an immutable characteristic or any reasons fundamental to their human dignity. If the Appellants do demonstrate that they are at risk of an honour crime, I do not find that they are at risk by virtue of being a member of that group. They would be at risk because they are being targeted by particular people, family members or others, who disagree with the marital situation before them. In my view, that risk falls within the purview of Section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee protection Act (IRPA). Credibility

The RPD did not err in its analysis of the Appellants' credibility. The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its assessment of their credibility by putting too much emphasis on an omission in their BOC, by not giving enough weight to their explanations for why they returned to Pakistan several times and by not properly assessing the letters from the Principal Appellant's lawyer and brother as well as his nephew's death certificate.

After conducting my own analysis and listening to the hearing recordings, I agree that the Appellants have not established that the Principal Appellant's ex-wife and in-laws have or will harm them. The evidence before me indicates that the Principal Appellant's in-laws are legally pursuing a disagreement over financial and material settlements related to the dissolution of the first arranged marriage in the appropriate court venues. As the RPD determined, discomfort and financial settlements related to the breakdown of a marriage contract are not akin to persecution.

The RPD correctly determined that the Appellants had not established that the Principal Appellant's in-laws sent a gunman to kill him nor that his in-laws killed his nephew. I have considered the evidence before me and come to the same conclusion as the RPD on these issues.

The Principal Appellant testified that in XXXX 2008, a gunman entered his family's yard late at night while his mother was praying. He was asleep. His mother screamed upon seeing the gunman which disturbed the neighbourhood and caused him to flee. The Principal Appellant never saw the gunman, the incident was never reported to the police and he returned to the UAE at the request of his parents who feared for his safety. The Appellants argue that the RPD did not give sufficient reasons for finding the incident not to be credible. They explain that the Principal Appellant had already received death threats prior to the gunman's arrival at their home, thus establishing a link that is more than subjective for believing the in-laws sent the gunman to kill him. Listening to the hearing recording, I note that the Principal Appellant never testified that he had received any threats prior to the gunman arriving and only indicated that he and his first wife had not been on good terms.1 In his BOC, he does allege that his in-laws threatened to kill him "whenever they can"2 but when asked about those threats during the hearing, his explanations did not establish on a balance of probabilities that there were actual life threats. During the hearing, the Principal Appellant responded that his ex-in-laws had tried to harm him financially and had also tried to kill him.3 When the Principal Appellant and the co-Appellant elaborated upon these threats, two incidents were mentioned - the XXXX incident with the gunman and the death of a nephew. Throughout the two hearings, all other threats were alleged to be either difficult discussions or financial requests largely pursued via the court or Jirga systems. In this case, I find that the Principal Appellant's estimation that the gunman was sent by his in-laws is subjective and related to the discomfort that he is feeling due to a contentious separation with his first wife.

The Principal Appellant shared a second incident where his nephew was allegedly killed by his in-laws following a dispute with his brothers-in-law. The Principal Appellant was not in Pakistan at the time. Since his and his first wife's families are related, he explained that his family was told by a common family member that his nephew was killed as revenge for defending him. In their memorandum on appeal, the Appellants focus their argument on the RPD's statement that "had his uncle received this information, there was no reason for his sister's family to contact every single authority, as stated in his narrative."4 I find that the Appellants have misapprehended the RPD's reasons for finding that the in-laws' involvement in the nephew's death had not been established. The RPD explained that the Principal Appellant had not indicated that the nephew had been killed by his in-laws in his BOC. In that document, he characterized that incident as a random killing where the suspects were unknown. "Three months back, my sister's son was killed by someone, in the daylight. His motorbike was also snatched. He was very young and had no enemies either. My sister's family contacted every single authority, yet nothing has happened so far and no one has been caught."5

During testimony, the Principal Appellant characterized this incident differently. He indicated that his nephew had defended him to his brothers-in-law and was killed. He testified that a few days after the death, a mutual maternal uncle had been told that his in-laws had his nephew killed. When the RPD confronted him about the difference between his BOC and his testimony, he did not explain the contradiction but rather spoke about his in-laws wanting a message to be conveyed to him. On appeal, the Appellants again focus on the importance of the Pashtun traditions, the propensity towards revenge and honour killings and the reasons why his in-laws would not hide their involvement in the killing. However, none of this explains the contradiction between his BOC and his testimony. This contradiction does not relate to the cultural context but to the Principal Appellant's own differing characterizations of the same incident. The Appellants have repeatedly failed to explain this inconsistency. I find that they have not established that the nephew was harmed by the Principal Appellant's in-laws.

I also find that the Appellants have misapprehended the reason why the RPD correctly gave the nephew's death certificate little weight. While it is evidence of the nephew's death, as argued by the Appellants on appeal, it is not evidence that the in-laws had him killed. This is reinforced by the fact that the death certificate indicates that the nature of the death was normal. The Appellant argues that his credibility should not be affected by his failure to explain in detail the content of a document that he did not produce. In fact, the RPD did not impugn his credibility for that reason and neither do I. I do note that the Appellant is responsible for establishing his story on a balance of probabilities. The document simply does not support his story that his nephew was murdered. This is why I assign no weight with respect to corroborating his story.

The RPD did not err by finding that the Appellants had not provided acceptable explanations for why they returned to Pakistan, given that they claim to fear for their lives at the hands of the Principal Appellant's ex-in-laws who are also his relatives. The Appellants argue that it is not unreasonable that they would want to preserve family relationships or meet with their lawyer in person. They argue that they only returned for brief visits to Islamabad and Peshawar, hours away from the Principal Appellant's hometown. However, they also argue that since the Principal Appellant's first wife is a relative, they could not hide their family in Islamabad or Peshawar.6 The Appellants' arguments on appeal are contradictory in that they claim to have taken precautions by visiting the very cities where they allege they could easily be found. I note that the co-Appellant testified that she returned to Pakistan so that her mother could receive care. However, the co-Appellant's mother lived in the UAE with her. Though the co-Appellant feared for her life, she still opted to return to Pakistan with her mother for medical treatment. And, if the Principal Appellant truly feared for his life, I find that it was not acceptable to visit Pakistan for an in-person meeting with a lawyer. Even in the case of a visit to a sick father, given that the Principal Appellant alleged a fear of harm to his life at the hands of family relations, a family visit would have facilitated his in-laws' access to him. I find that given the fears that they have expressed, the Appellants have not credibly explained why they visited Pakistan many times since XXXX 2008, including 8-10 visits for the Principal Appellant alone. Corroborating evidence

I find that the RPD did not err in its appreciation of any corroborating evidence. The Appellants allege that the RPD failed to properly appreciate evidence, including letters from their lawyer and the Principal Appellant's brother in law which attest to the Principal Appellant's in-laws having threatened his life. Excerpt from letter from lawyer "It is highly important to mention here that the other party is not only showing a non-serious behaviour and practising boycott of Mr. XXXX family, they have also been using harsh words outside the court room. At many occasions, they misbehaved with Mr. XXXX mother and have them life threats especially for Mr. XXXX and his second family (second wife and children). I can see lack of education and impact of the common social culture, in their conduct. Their defeat in the family court, where the case took several years to resolve, has further aroused their unwanted anger, and they appear to be even more revengeful now."7 Excerpt from letter from brother-in-law "It is important to mention here that despite accepting all valid demands of XXXX family and extending complete cooperation to them, there has been an unending chain of ill conducts, maltreatments and threats going on from her father and 7 brothers. It has reached to a point where XXXX second wife, XXXX XXXX and there [sic] 2 sons are facing life threats from them. Further to this there have been 2 major incidents in the past, i.e. the attempt of physical attack on XXXX (2008) and his nephew's murder (2017) that have worsen the situation for XXXX second family."8

I note that in the letter from the lawyer, there is no mention of threats made against the Appellants in court, as alleged in their testimony.9 Moreover, though life threats are mentioned, the lawyer does not specify what the threats are and how they occurred. The letter from the brother-in-law also speaks to life threats directly affecting the co-Appellant and her children. Again, the letter does not specify what these life threats are. Furthermore, the brother-in-law mentions the two incidents that the Principal Appellant presented before the RPD. Both my analysis and the RPD's analysis have concluded that the Appellants have not established that these incidents were carried out by the Pashtun in-laws on a balance of probabilities. The brother-in-law's letter does not add information that speaks to a different conclusion. The co-Appellant testified that she received a call from the Principal Appellant's first father-in-law but characterized that call as an attempt to scare them that did not contain life threats.10 When looking at the various corroborating documents, I do not find that they establish that the Appellants are actually facing life threats on a balance of probabilities. I also assign them no weight with respect to establishing that fact.

The Appellants submitted several articles11 stating that people from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have been killed on the orders of a Jirga tribal council for engaging in free will marriages or refusing forced marriages. The articles state that these killings have occurred both within and outside of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa but that the victims were mainly of Pashtun descent. However, in the Appellants' case, a Jirga twice evaluated the situation and did not order any killing. The Appellants testified that the Jirga requested that the Principal Appellant pay an amount to his ex-wife's family to compensate for his having left his first wife in the care of his in-laws. The Principal Appellant's in-laws then pursued the case in Pakistan's official judicial system. Various judgements and petitions12 stemming from these courts have obliged the Principal Appellant to pay his first wife compensation, and have determined that she is not obliged to life with him and have returned the case to a lower court for redetermination following appeals by his first wife. The evidence before me does not indicate that the Principal Appellant's in-laws are pursuing the avenues of harm described in the articles. The evidence indicates that the Principal Appellant's first wife is dissatisfied with the negotiations over the equivalent of alimony/child support payments, the return of the dowry, the reimbursement for the birth of their child and alleged mistreatment. In those court documents, she alleges that the lower court failed to properly appreciate the evidence before it. The higher court allowed the appeal and returned the case to the trial lower court. In this evidence and official documentation, the Principal Appellant's lawyer does not allege that in-laws have attempted to harm him. These documents do capture the first wife's complaint of mistreatment at the hands of the Principal Appellant's family. I find that if the Principal Appellant's in-laws were threatening him in court in front of their lawyer, as alleged by the Appellants during his testimony, these allegations would have been captured by those documents.

The corroborating evidence before me does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants are facing any physical threats to their lives from the Principal Appellant's first wife and her family.

Based on the evidence before me, I conclude that the Appellants have not established their allegations of threats from their in-laws on a balance of probabilities. Section 96: Fear of Gender-based Violence

The Co-Appellant alleges a fear of gender-based violence as a result of the threats from her husband's ex-in-laws as well as a fear of returning to Pakistani society as an independent woman who does not fit in and conform to societal norms. I have confirmed that the RPD did not err by finding that the Appellants have not established a threat from the Principal Appellant's ex-in-laws. I also find that the RPD did not err in its analysis of the Co-Appellant's risk of harm related to her return to Pakistani society.

The Appellants argue that the RPD did not turn its mind to whether Pakistani society rejects women who consider themselves to be independent and thus, failed in its analysis. The Appellants argue that numerous documents in the National Documentation Package (NDP) make it clear that women who do not follow the rules set out for women in Pakistan face a risk of violence. However, in their memorandum, they have not indicated where in the NDP this is indicated. They also argue that RPD exhibits E-15 through E-21 demonstrate the risk of violence that women face. Exhibits E-15 through E-21 are articles speaking to various honour killings that have occurred. While I do not deny that honour killings can and do occur in Pakistan, my analysis has revealed that the Co-Appellant does not face that risk. The evidence before me establishes that, on a balance of probabilities, no one has threatened her, her husband, or her children with repercussions and harm related to the threat of an honour killing.

Concerning the general treatment of women in Pakistani society, the NDP does indicate that the level of discrimination against women does not in general amount to persecution.13 The Co-Appellant has not credibly established other grounds that would justify protection under Section 96 of the IRPA.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
